newsitem.title: CROATIA: Croat opposition figure slammed for tribunal talks.
newsitem.headline: Croat opposition figure slammed for tribunal talks.

text.p: State-run Croatian newspapers on Friday described a well-known opposition figure as a traitor for having allegedly given evidence to the U.N. war crimes tribunal against President Franjo Tudjman.

They published extracts of what they said was an interview given to tribunal officials by Stipe Mesic, the last head of former Yugoslavia's collective presidency, together with photographs of a statement signed by him.

But Mesic, a former prominent member of Tudjman's party who broke away to form an opposition party in 1994, told journalists he had not given evidence to the court itself, but rather only tribunal representatives.
He also said Friday's newspaper articles omitted most of the part of his interview in which he blamed Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic for starting the wars that broke up federal Yugoslavia.

"I have never been to The Hague. I never testified. I spoke with official ICTY representatives who invited me and asked if I could say something about the fall of Yugoslavia as the last president of the former Yugoslavia.
"I agreed to be interviewed, but this was not my initiative," Mesic told journalists.

"(What has been published) are only fragments which are marginal. The main elements have been omitted such as my condemnation of Milosevic's policy and those who enabled him to implement it," he said.
"I said Slobodan Milosevic planned and started the war and I thought he should answer for that before the Hague Tribunal as a war criminal."
The coordinated release of the documents suggested an attempt to discredit Mesic, though he said he doubted Tudjman was personally involved.
Formerly a close associate of Tudjman, Mesic fell out with him over the nationalist president's interventionist policy towards Bosnia and formed an independent party.
"I don't think the very top people are behind this, but corrupt individuals who think they can form a little group around Tudjman and score points," said Mesic.

Mesic has never hidden his views of Tudjman's role in the wars in former Yugoslavia that broke out after four of the federation's six republics, including Croatia under Tudjman and Bosnia, declared independence in 1991-92.
Mesic spoke in the published excerpts of meetings held between Tudjman and Milosevic throughout the 1991-95 war.

He quoted Tudjman as saying: "What we are holding by force will be ours," referring to parts of Bosnia then occupied by Croatian government troops and the Bosnian Croat militia, which was armed by Zagreb.
"I took this to mean it would become Croatian territory, though it wasn't said explicitly," Mesic was reported by the newspapers as saying.
Editorial comments referred to the interview as evidence of a prosecution witness despite Mesic never having been called in front of the international court.
A spokesman for the tribunal told Reuters that the court had absolutely no comment to make.
Tudjman is known to have used the back of a menu at a formal dinner in London in May 1995 to illustrate his prediction of a Bosnia divided between Serbia and Croatia.
The sketch showed the Bosnian border as it was then, cut in two by an S-shaped line. Arrows showed one side going to Croatia and the other to Serbia.
Western analysts portrayed this as evidence of a Tudjman-Milosevic deal to redraw Bosnia's map, absorbing its Moslems into what Tudjman called the Croat Federation.
Postwar Bosnia is effectively divided into Moslem, Serbian- and Croatian-dominated spheres.
One diplomat told Reuters: "These allegations (of Tudjman-Milosevic designs on Bosnia)...have been bar talk for many years now. There is nothing novel in them.
"(But) the Croatian government will have been deeply stung that one of their own politicians has had the nerve to go off and talk to The Hague (officials)."
